0.title: What a Man Tells Himself
0.essay:
Every man carries a running commentary in his head. Much of it he picked up long ago: from a father, a coach, a playground, a film, a first job. Some of it is true. Some of it is a lie he has believed for so long that it simply sounds like the way things are.

Lies that sound like common sense

The lies in this study rarely announce themselves. They sound like maturity: “I’ll deal with it myself.” They sound like responsibility: “I have to keep working.” They sound like honesty: “That’s just how I am.” Most of them are half-truths, which is why they are so believable. A whole lie is easy to spot. A half-truth borrows the strength of the true half to carry the false one.

Jesus said, “you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:32). He said it to people who thought they were already free. That is often where men stand: unaware of the bars because they have lived behind them for years.

Tendencies, not rules

These chapters are written for men, single and married, young and older. Women believe many of these lies too, and plenty of men will not recognise themselves in every chapter. These are tendencies, not rules. The companion study Lies Women Tell Themselves takes up a different set. Nothing here is meant to mock. Every lie is answered first with Scripture, and then with Christ, who is not only the truth about God but the truth about what a man is meant to be. The study Biblical Manhood sets out that calling in full; this study listens to the voices that pull against it.

The chapters

“I Don’t Need Anyone”; “I Am What I Achieve”; “It’s Just How I’m Made”; Two Lies About Leading; “It’s Too Late for Me”; and Trading Lies for Truth.

For reflection

What sentences about being a man did you hear most often growing up? Which of them still speak loudest in your head, and do you know which half is true?

1.title: “I Don’t Need Anyone”
1.essay:
“I’m fine.” It may be the most common lie men tell, and the one they tell themselves first. Behind it stand two older lies: a real man does not show weakness, and a real man does not need anyone.

The lie in a man’s own words

It sounds like this. Keep it together. Don’t make a fuss. Nobody wants to hear about it. If I admit I’m struggling, people will think less of me. I’ve always sorted my own problems out. Some men learned it in a house where tears were punished or mocked. Some learned it in a changing room, a barracks or an office. Many simply never saw another man say, “I’m not coping.”

Why it is believable

Here is the true half. Scripture does call men to strength. Paul writes, “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love” (1 Corinthians 16:13–14). Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit, and there are times to hold your feelings back for the sake of others: a father in a crisis, a man at his post. Steadiness is a gift.

The lie takes that good thing and turns it inside out. It makes strength mean never being seen to need. It confuses composure with concealment. And it quietly assumes that a man’s worth rests on how capable he looks.

Strong men in Scripture wept

The Bible’s strongest men were not ashamed of tears. David, a warrior who killed a giant, could write, “every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping” (Psalm 6:6). When he and Jonathan parted, “they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most” (1 Samuel 20:41). When Peter realised what he had done, “he went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75).

And at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, knowing he was about to raise him, the Son of God stood and grieved. “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In Gethsemane he did not hide his distress from his closest friends. He said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). The perfect man asked for company in his darkest hour. If he did, you may.

The strength God gives

Paul had a weakness he begged God to remove. God refused, and told him why: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul’s conclusion turns the lie upside down: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). A man who will not admit weakness is relying on the one resource that will certainly run out: himself. A man who admits it has access to a power that never will.

Made for brothers

The second lie is close kin to the first. Many men have colleagues, teammates and a wife, but no friend who knows what is really going on inside them. Friendships fade as marriage, children and career fill the diary, and isolation creeps in unchosen.

God said at the beginning, “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). The Preacher puts it bluntly: “Two are better than one … For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10). Isolation is not neutral. “Whoever isolates himself seeks his own desire” (Proverbs 18:1). Alone, a man’s thinking narrows, his temptations grow louder, and his low moods have no one to interrupt them.

Look at the friendships Scripture honours. When David was hunted, Jonathan “went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). Paul, who faced mobs, prisons and shipwrecks, was constantly asking for his friends. Near the end he writes, “Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you” (2 Timothy 4:11). He thanks God for Onesiphorus, who “often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains” (2 Timothy 1:16). He even says that God “comforts the downcast” by sending a friend (2 Corinthians 7:6).

An example

A man in his forties loses his job and tells nobody at church for three months. He leaves the house each morning in a suit. When a friend finally guesses, the man is angry, then relieved, then in tears in a car park. “I thought I had to fix it before anyone found out,” he says. The friend does not fix it either. But the next Sunday two other men take him for breakfast, and one of them has been through the same thing.

What Christ says to him

Jesus does not say, “Pull yourself together.” He says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). We have a high priest who is able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). He has called his disciples friends (John 15:15). The man who thinks he must carry everything alone has never been asked to. The study Friendship & Hospitality has much more on how friendships are made and kept.

For reflection

When did you last tell someone the truth about how you were really doing? Who taught you that strength means never needing help? Is there one man you could take one step closer to this month? What does it mean to you that Jesus asked his friends to stay with him?

2.title: “I Am What I Achieve”
2.essay:
Ask a man who he is, and he will usually tell you what he does. But for many men the answer goes deeper than they realise: what I do, earn and build is not just my work. It is my worth.

The lie in a man’s own words

If I’m not providing, I’m nothing. A good month means I’m a good man; a bad month means I’m a failure. I’ll slow down once I’ve made it. My family needs me to keep climbing. For some men it is the salary. For others it is the title, the business, the trophies, the house, or simply being the one everyone relies on. For the unemployed, the retired and the ill, the same lie turns cruel: I’m no use to anyone now.

Why it is believable

The true half is large. God made man to work. He put Adam in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), and work is good, not a curse. Providing for those in your care is a serious duty. Excellence honours God. The study Christian at Work shows how every honest job can be done for the Lord.

The lie does not deny any of that. It simply moves work from the place of a calling to the place of a saviour. Work stops being something I do for God and others and becomes the thing that tells me I am all right.

A king who had it all

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes ran the experiment further than most of us can. He built houses, planted vineyards, gathered silver and gold, and “whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them” (Ecclesiastes 2:10). Then he stepped back: “Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11). Achievement could not hold the weight of a life. Worse, it robbed him of rest: “Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 2:23).

Yet the same book does not despise work. “There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Work is a good gift to enjoy. It is a terrible god to serve.

The man with bigger barns

Jesus told a story about a successful farmer. His harvest was so large that he planned to pull down his barns and build bigger ones, and then say to himself, “Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry” (Luke 12:19). He is not a thief, just a hard worker with a sensible plan. “But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’” (Luke 12:20).

Jesus introduced the story with a warning: “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). And he ended it: “So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:21). The farmer’s real failure was not his barns. It was that his whole sense of security was stored in them.

What it costs

This lie has victims. It is the father who is always at work and calls it love. It is the husband whose wife has been lonely for years in a comfortable house. It is the man who checks his phone through his children’s concerts. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Jesus asks the question that every driven man should hear: “For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). The study Busy, Tired & Restless takes up overwork and rest more fully.

An example

A self-employed builder in his fifties has worked six days a week for thirty years. When a back injury stops him for six months, he sinks lower than he has ever been. “I don’t know who I am if I’m not working,” he tells his pastor. Slowly, over that half year, he discovers that his grandchildren like him as much on the sofa as on the scaffolding, and that God has not loved him any less in the weeks he could do nothing at all.

What Christ says to him

The gospel turns this lie round. In Christ a man’s worth is received before it is achieved. At his baptism, before Jesus had preached or healed anyone, the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Everyone joined to Christ by faith stands in that same delight. Paul, who worked harder than almost anyone, knew where his identity came from: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

That frees a man to work hard without being driven, and to stop without falling apart. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men … You are serving the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:23–24). A man who works for Christ, rather than for his own sense of worth, can lose a job, retire, fall ill or fail in business, and still know exactly who he is.

For reflection

If your income or role disappeared tomorrow, what would you feel you had lost? Who in your life is paying the price for your work? Where do you most struggle to rest? What would it mean to hear the Father’s “well pleased” as spoken over you in Christ, before you do anything this week?

3.title: “It’s Just How I’m Made”
3.essay:
Some lies excuse a sin by making it small. Others excuse it by making it inevitable. Two of the most common among men do both: “I can handle my lust on my own, it isn’t that serious,” and “My anger is just how I am.”

The lie in a man’s own words

Every man looks at that stuff. It doesn’t hurt anyone. I’ll stop when I’m married, or when things are less stressful. It’s between me and God; nobody else needs to know. And on the other side: I’ve always had a temper. My dad was the same. I’m not violent, I just shout sometimes. They know I don’t mean it.

Why it is believable

Again there is a true half. Sexual desire is God’s good gift, and noticing beauty is not in itself sin; the study Attraction & a Clean Conscience explains that carefully, and frees men from false guilt. Temperament is real too: some men are more easily stirred than others, and family patterns run deep. Scripture itself says, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26). So the lie can sound like plain realism.

But it hides two things. It hides the seriousness of sin, and it hides the way sin grows in the dark.

Not that serious?

Jesus did not treat lust as a small thing. “But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). He told men to deal with it radically, as if tearing out an eye. That is not because he despises men’s bodies, but because he loves them, and the women they look at, who are someone’s daughters and sisters, made in God’s image.

James shows how sin grows: “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:14–15). A habit that feels manageable at twenty can have hold of a man at fifty. “Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned?” (Proverbs 6:27).

The same goes for anger. “Just how I am” sounds honest, but it is a refusal to change. “For the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). Those who live with an angry man usually know better than he does how much it hurts. Temperament may explain a struggle; it never excuses it. The study Anger traces where anger comes from and how it can be spent at the cross.

Alone is where it wins

Notice what both lies have in common: they keep a man on his own. “I can handle it.” “Nobody else needs to know.” “It’s my business.” This is the first lie of this study again, in a different form. And secrecy is the soil sin grows best in.

David knew it. “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). Only when he stopped covering it did relief come: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5). “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

And James adds the step most men avoid: “Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Confession to God brings forgiveness. Confession to a trusted brother very often brings healing: the power of the secret is broken, and someone can now pray, ask and help. The study Fighting Sin & Temptation sets out how this works in practice.

An example

A young married man has used pornography since he was thirteen. He has confessed it to God hundreds of times and promised himself hundreds of times that this was the last. One evening, shaking, he tells an older man from church. The older man says, “Thank you for trusting me. I’ve fought this too.” They agree to meet every fortnight. He still struggles, but for the first time in fifteen years he is not fighting alone, and the falls grow further apart. Later, with help, he tells his wife.

What Christ says to him

Christ does not wink at these sins, and he does not walk away from the men who commit them. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Faithful and just: forgiveness rests not on how sorry you feel but on the blood of Jesus, which “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). He bore the shame you are hiding. He does not need you to clean yourself up before you come.

And he gives his Spirit, whose fruit includes “gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:23). A man is not stuck with “how I am”. In Christ he is “a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17), and the Spirit is at work making him gentler and freer than he has ever been.

If your anger has ever frightened your wife or children, or crossed into hitting, threatening or controlling, that is abuse. Stop, tell your pastor, and get specialist help now. Their safety comes first.

For reflection

What sin in your life do you most often call “not that serious” or “just how I am”? Who knows about it? Is there one trustworthy brother you could tell this month? How does 1 John 1:9 speak to the shame that keeps you silent?

4.title: Two Lies About Leading
4.essay:
Men tend to believe one of two opposite lies about leadership. The first says, “Being a man means being in control, and leading means getting my way.” The second says, “I’m just not cut out to lead, not at home and not in church.” One produces tyrants; the other, absent men. Christ answers both.

The first lie: control

I’m the head of this house, so what I say goes. If I give ground, I lose respect. A real man is in charge. It can be loud, in shouting and demands, or quiet, in controlling the money, sulking until he gets his way, or never asking his wife what she thinks.

The true half is that this commentary believes God does give husbands a real responsibility to lead in the home, and gives the oversight of the church to qualified men (see Biblical Manhood, and the entries on headship and women in ministry in Positions at a Glance). Many Christians, usually called egalitarians, read those passages differently, and the study Biblical Manhood sets out both views fairly. But on this point both views agree completely: Christian leadership is never domination.

Not so among you

When the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus said, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:42–45).

That defines everything. Paul does not tell husbands to make their wives submit. He tells them, “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and “do not be harsh with them” (Colossians 3:19). Elders must not be “domineering over those in your charge” (1 Peter 5:3). The measure of a leader is not how often he gets his way, but how much he gives himself away. Jesus, knowing “that the Father had given all things into his hands”, took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:3–5). Authority, in his hands, kneels.

Let this be said plainly. Using headship to control, intimidate, threaten or hurt a wife or children is abuse. It is never tolerated, and it is a lie about Christ. Anyone suffering abuse should seek safety at once and report it to the authorities. A man who recognises himself here must stop, tell someone, and get help now.

The second lie: “Not me”

My wife is more spiritual than I am. I wouldn’t know what to say. I can’t pray out loud. Other men are better at this. Leave it to the pastor. This lie is often more common than the first, and it sounds humble. In truth it is often fear, sometimes laziness, and sometimes an old wound of having been told you were not good enough.

Moses knew this lie well. “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11). “Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent” (Exodus 4:10). And finally the honest one: “Oh, my Lord, please send someone else” (Exodus 4:13). God’s answer was not, “Yes, you are very gifted.” It was, “But I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). Gideon said his clan was the weakest and he was the least; God said the same thing (Judges 6:15–16).

Ordinary faithfulness

Spiritual leadership in a home is mostly small and repeated. “You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). That is a conversation in the car, a short prayer at a meal, a Bible story at bedtime, getting everyone to church on a tired Sunday, and saying “I was wrong” first. It needs no eloquence, only a man who turns up.

This is not only for husbands and fathers. A single man leads when he takes responsibility for his own walk with God, serves without being asked, encourages a younger believer, prays with a friend, and sets an example in his church. Jesus himself was unmarried, and so was the apostle Paul. The study Singleness treats that calling with honour.

An example

A man in his thirties has always left the spiritual side of family life to his wife, who grew up in church while he did not. One evening his eight-year-old asks him to pray at bedtime. He stumbles through three sentences. His son says, “That was good, Dad.” He starts reading a short psalm with the children after dinner. His wife tells a friend it is the most attractive thing he has done in years.

What Christ says to him

To the controlling man Christ says: look at me with a towel, and learn from me, “for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). To the absent man he says what he said to Moses: I will be with you. To both he offers himself as the leader who never failed, who laid down his life for his bride. A man does not lead well by trying harder to be impressive. He leads well by following Christ closely enough that others can follow him.

For reflection

Which of the two lies do you lean towards: control or absence? How would the people closest to you answer that question? What is one small act of servant leadership you could begin this week? Where have you been saying “send someone else”?

5.title: “It’s Too Late for Me”
5.essay:
Some men are not driven, controlling or proud. They are simply defeated. They look back at a marriage that ended, children who will not speak to them, years lost to drink or work or a secret, and they conclude: I have failed too badly. It is too late for me.

The lie in a man’s own words

I had my chance and I blew it. God might forgive other people, but not after what I did. I’m too old to change now. I can never lead or serve again. Best to keep my head down and get to the end.

Why it is believable

The true half is painful. Some things cannot be undone. Words cannot be unsaid, years cannot be relived, and sin often leaves consequences that remain long after it is forgiven. A man who has done real harm should feel the weight of it. Scripture never asks him to pretend otherwise. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

The lie takes that true grief and draws a false conclusion from it: because I cannot undo it, God cannot redeem it. It sets a limit on grace and calls the limit realism. Often it is mixed with a man’s pride, too, which would rather stay condemned than receive mercy he did not earn.

Men who were not too far gone

Manasseh, king of Judah, was one of the worst kings Judah ever had. He filled Jerusalem with idols and “burned his sons as an offering in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom” (2 Chronicles 33:6). Yet when God brought him low, “he entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly … and God was moved by his entreaty and heard his plea” (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Late in life, after decades of evil, he was received.

A criminal was dying on a cross beside Jesus. He had no time left to make amends, attend church or prove himself. He had only one sentence: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” And Jesus answered, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). It was not too late, with hours to live.

Peter denied Jesus three times on the night he needed him most. Afterwards the risen Lord met him by a charcoal fire and gave him work to do: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Paul, who had hunted Christians, called himself the foremost of sinners, and then explained why God saved him: “that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). Your story, too, can become a display of that patience. The study Regret & the Past walks slowly through these stories and the long work of living with what cannot be undone.

Never too late to begin

It is never too late to come to Christ. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). It is never too late to confess, to apologise, to make what amends are possible, and to begin doing what is right today. An estranged son may not answer the first letter, or the fifth. A former wife may rightly want no contact, and that must be respected. But a man can still pray for them, honour them, and become a different man whether or not they ever see it.

And it is never too late to be useful. Some of the most valuable men in any church are older men who have failed, been forgiven, and now speak to younger men with a humility that only failure teaches. The study Growing Old Well has more on finishing well.

An example

A man of sixty-five spent his twenties and thirties drinking, and his children grew up afraid of him. He became a Christian at fifty-eight. His daughter will see him now, carefully. His son will not. He has written to his son twice, owning what he did without excuses, and asking nothing. Meanwhile he volunteers at a recovery group at his church. “I can’t give my kids their childhood back,” he says. “But I can tell these younger men the truth before they lose theirs.”

What Christ says to him

To the man who says it is too late, Christ says: I came for exactly you. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15). His blood does not run out at a certain age or a certain number of failures. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). And the God who promised his people, “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (Joel 2:25), is still able to bring good out of wasted years, often in ways a man could never have planned.

If the weight of the past has become despair, and you have begun to think others would be better off without you, please read the last chapter of this study now, and tell someone today.

For reflection

What failure in your past most often whispers, “It’s too late”? Which of the men in this chapter is most like you? What would it look like to take one step of repentance or repair this week, without demanding a particular result? How does 1 Timothy 1:15–16 speak to you?

6.title: Trading Lies for Truth
6.essay:
Lies are not defeated by being noticed once. They have usually been rehearsed for years, and they need to be answered for years. This last chapter is about how a man replaces the old voices with the truth, and when he needs more help than a book can give.

Where lies come from

The first lie in the Bible was a half-truth: “You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:4–5). Their eyes were opened, and it was a disaster. Jesus calls the devil “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). Many of the lies in a man’s head come from the world, his family and his own heart, which is “deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9), but the enemy is glad to use them all. They work the same way: by taking something true and bending it.

Renewing the mind

Paul writes, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Renewal is a process, not an event. It happens by soaking the mind in Scripture until God’s voice becomes louder than the old ones.

In practice this means three steps. First, name the lie: write down the sentence you actually tell yourself, in your own words. “I’m on my own.” “I’m only worth what I earn.” Second, answer it with Scripture, not with positive thinking. Find the verse that speaks most directly to it and learn it by heart. Third, turn to Christ: pray it back to him, thanking him that the truth is not only a sentence but a person. Paul calls this to “take every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). It is a fight, but a winnable one, because the Spirit of truth lives in every believer.

Brothers who tell the truth

No man can see all his own lies. That is why God gives brothers. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6). “Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17). “Exhort one another every day … that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13).

Every man needs at least one or two other men who know him well and have permission to ask hard questions. Not a group where everyone reports success, but a friendship where it is safe to say, “I fell again.” Such friendships are usually built slowly, over shared work, meals and prayer, in a local church. If you have none, ask your pastor to help you find one, and be willing to go first.

When you need more help

Some of what this study has touched on can become more than a struggle. Please do not let the lie “I can handle it alone” keep you from help.

If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone now. In many countries men take their own lives around three times as often as women, often without telling anyone first. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), or go to your nearest emergency department. Then tell someone you trust, and see a doctor. Asking for help is not weakness or unbelief. Your life is precious to God, and you are not a burden to the people who love you. The study Depression & the Christian is written for those in that darkness.

If you are low for weeks, sleeping badly, losing interest in everything, or drinking more to cope, see a doctor. Depression in men often shows itself as irritability, overwork or numbness rather than sadness. Medicine and counselling are no failure of faith.

If you are caught in an addiction, whether to alcohol, drugs, gambling or pornography, you will need more than willpower. Tell a trusted Christian, involve your pastor, and seek specialist help.

If you are being abused, by a partner or anyone else, men can be victims too. Seek safety and tell someone. If you are the one causing harm, hitting, threatening, controlling or frightening those at home, stop, tell your pastor, accept accountability, and get specialist help now. The safety of your wife and children comes before your reputation. Real repentance welcomes accountability; it does not demand quick trust.

An example

A young man keeps a note on his phone titled “Lies.” Under each lie he writes a verse. “I’m on my own”: Hebrews 13:5. “I’m only what I achieve”: 1 Corinthians 15:10. “It’s too late”: John 6:37. He reads it on the train most mornings. Every few weeks he and a friend from church go through it together and add a line. He says it has done more for him than any resolution he ever made.

The truth is a person

In the end, the answer to every lie in this study is not a technique but Jesus Christ, who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). In him a man sees what strength really is: tears at a grave, a towel at a supper, a cross for his bride. In him a man is forgiven, adopted, given brothers and given work to do. The lies say you must prove yourself, protect yourself and save yourself. Christ says it is finished, and invites you to follow him. For a book-length treatment of these themes, many men have found Robert Wolgemuth’s Lies Men Believe helpful.

For reflection

Which lie from this study do you most need to answer, and with which verse? Who are the brothers in your life who would tell you the truth? Is there anything in the “more help” section above that you have been avoiding? What does it mean to you that the truth that sets you free is a person who loves you?
